10. Comparability Over Time and Space

Satellite data were collected by several different satellite altimeters over different time spans. Steps have been taken to calibrate the results and remove biases over time, and NOAA made sure to restrict its analysis to the portion of the globe between 66 degrees south and 66 degrees north, where coverage is most complete. The number of tide gauges collecting data has changed over time, but the methods used to reconstruct a long-term time series adjust for these changes. The most notable difference between the two observed time series displayed in the graph is that the long-term reconstruction includes a glacial isostatic adjustment correction, while the altimeter series does not. The technical documentation for the Sea Level indicator explains the distinction and the rationale for leaving it in place.

All of the tide gauges included in the map have used the same methods for determining hourly water levels. These methods remained constant over time and across gauges, except as documented in NOAA (2014). The map has been limited to stations that have collected data consistently throughout the 60+-year period of interest.

The observed and projected time series cover the same spatial extent: a time series that is representative of the global ocean overall (though with the satellite coverage limitations noted above) and relative sea level changes for the same set of tide gauge stations.

11. Data Limitations

The technical documentation for the Sea Level indicator identifies some factors that may impact the confidence, application, or conclusions that readers can draw from the observed portion of this pairing. For example, most satellite altimeter tracks span the area from 66 degrees north latitude to 66 degrees south, so they cover about 90 percent of the ocean surface, not the entire ocean. The satellite record alone is not long enough to distinguish medium-term variability from long-term change, which is why it has been supplemented with a longer-term reconstruction based on tide gauge measurements. Projections of relative sea level must make assumptions about vertical land motion, among other factors, based in part on historical observations.

12. Sources of Uncertainty

Observations inevitably reflect measurement uncertainty. The technical documentation for the Sea Level indicator provides a detailed assessment of such uncertainties, including reported error bounds for observed trends based on tide gauges, satellite altimeter uncertainty, an acknowledged ongoing debate about how best to reconstruct global mean sea level change from tide gauge records, and a discussion of how various studies are progressively “closing the gap” between different methods of measuring sea level change.

Interpreting projections requires users to consider scenario uncertainty. Projecting future conditions requires assumptions about future greenhouse gas emissions. This feature presents two widely used scenarios to illustrate a range of possibilities without assigning likelihoods to them, nor do these scenarios necessarily bound possible futures.

Sweet et al. (2022) discuss additional sources of uncertainty associated with projecting sea level rise and translating from global to regional estimates.

13. Sources of Variability

Changes in sea level can be influenced by multi-year cycles such as El Niño/La Niña and the Pacific Decadal Oscillation, which affect coastal ocean temperatures, salt content, winds, atmospheric pressure, and currents. The construction of this pairing addresses variability in a few ways:

  • Supplementing the satellite record with a longer-term reconstruction based on tide gauges.
  • Reporting total change over long timeframes.
  • Presenting projections at decadal time intervals.
